Rioja.climate: Continental, tempered by the Atlantic via the Ebro valley
Rioja.agingRules: Crianza: 2yr total, min 1 in oak. Reserva: 3yr, min 1 in oak. Gran Reserva: 5yr, min 2 in oak.

Ribera del Duero.climate: High-altitude continental — big diurnal swings concentrate skins
Ribera del Duero.agingRules: Same Crianza/Reserva/Gran Reserva ladder as Rioja

Burgundy.classification: AOC, with Grand Cru/Premier Cru/Village/Regional tiers
Burgundy.climate: Cool continental — vintage variation is large and prices track it
Burgundy.agingRules: No fixed cellar mandate; single-vineyard Grand Cru sits atop a strict site-based hierarchy, not a time-in-barrel rule

Bordeaux.classification: AOC, Left Bank vs Right Bank, 1855 Classification for Médoc
Bordeaux.climate: Maritime, moderated by the Gironde estuary
Bordeaux.agingRules: Blends vary by bank: Left Bank (gravel, Médoc) leans Cabernet-dominant; Right Bank (clay, Pomerol/St-Émilion) leans Merlot-dominant

Napa Valley.climate: Warm days, fog-cooled nights off San Pablo Bay
Napa Valley.agingRules: No formal aging mandate — house style sets it, often riper and more oak-forward than Bordeaux

Piedmont.climate: Foggy, cool continental in the Langhe hills
Piedmont.agingRules: Barolo: min 38 months aging, 18 in wood. Barbaresco: min 26 months, 9 in wood.

Tuscany.classification: DOCG (Chianti Classico, Brunello di Montalcino) / DOC
Tuscany.climate: Warm Mediterranean, tempered by hillside altitude and sea breezes
Tuscany.agingRules: Chianti Classico Riserva: min 24 months. Brunello di Montalcino: min 5 years, at least 2 in oak.

Marlborough.climate: Sunny days, cold nights, maritime — locks in high acidity and pyrazine aromatics
Marlborough.agingRules: Not aging-focused — drunk young for freshness

Champagne.climate: Marginal cool climate — grapes barely ripen, which is what makes the base wine right for sparkling
Champagne.agingRules: Non-vintage: min 15 months on lees (12 by law, house minimums run higher). Vintage: min 3 years.

Loire Valley.agingRules: No aging mandate; Sancerre is a flint-and-citrus style meant young

Provence.agingRules: No aging mandate — pale, dry rosé built for immediate drinking

Rhône Valley.classification: AOC (Côtes du Rhône, crus such as Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Hermitage)
Rhône Valley.climate: Continental in the north, warm Mediterranean in the south
Rhône Valley.agingRules: No general ageing mandate; each cru sets its own rules

Alsace.classification: AOC Alsace, with 51 Grand Cru vineyards
Alsace.climate: Cool continental, sheltered and dry in the rain shadow of the Vosges
Alsace.agingRules: No ageing mandate; wines are labelled by grape, unusually for France

Beaujolais.classification: AOC Beaujolais, Beaujolais-Villages and ten crus
Beaujolais.climate: Semi-continental, warmer than Burgundy to the north
Beaujolais.agingRules: No ageing mandate; Beaujolais Nouveau is released in November of the harvest year

Languedoc-Roussillon.classification: AOC Languedoc and Roussillon appellations, plus IGP Pays d'Oc

Chablis.classification: AOC, with Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru tiers
Chablis.climate: Cool continental, with frost a regular risk
Chablis.agingRules: No fixed ageing mandate; many producers use little or no new oak

Veneto.classification: DOC and DOCG (Valpolicella, Amarone della Valpolicella, Soave, Prosecco Superiore)
Veneto.climate: Continental, moderated by Lake Garda and the Adriatic
Veneto.agingRules: Amarone della Valpolicella must age at least 2 years before release, 4 for Riserva

Sicily.classification: DOC Sicilia, Etna DOC, Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG, Marsala DOC
Sicily.climate: Hot Mediterranean, cooler at altitude on Mount Etna

Puglia.classification: DOC (Primitivo di Manduria, Salice Salentino) and IGP Puglia

Abruzzo.classification: DOC Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and Trebbiano d'Abruzzo, Colline Teramane DOCG
Abruzzo.climate: Mediterranean on the coast, cooler towards the Apennines
Abruzzo.agingRules: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Riserva must age at least 2 years

Friuli-Venezia Giulia.classification: DOC (Collio, Friuli Colli Orientali, Friuli Grave)
Friuli-Venezia Giulia.climate: Cool, between the Alps and the Adriatic

Trentino-Alto Adige.classification: DOC Alto Adige (Südtirol) and Trentino, Trento DOC for sparkling

Campania.classification: DOCG Taurasi, Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo
Campania.climate: Mediterranean, cooler in the hills around Avellino
Campania.agingRules: Taurasi must age at least 3 years, with 1 in wood

Priorat.classification: DOQ (DOCa), one of only two in Spain
Priorat.climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean with steep slate (llicorella) slopes
Priorat.agingRules: No general ageing mandate beyond the Spanish Crianza/Reserva terms

Rías Baixas.agingRules: No ageing mandate; mostly made for drinking young

Jerez.climate: Hot and dry, with Atlantic breezes and chalky albariza soil
Jerez.agingRules: Sherry must age at least 2 years in the solera system

Penedès.classification: DO Penedès; most Cava DO also comes from here
Penedès.agingRules: Cava must age at least 9 months on its lees

Rueda.climate: Continental, hot days and cold nights on a high plateau

Douro.classification: DOC Douro for table wine and DOC Porto for Port
Douro.climate: Hot, dry continental with steep schist terraces
Douro.agingRules: Vintage Port is bottled after about 2 years in barrel; tawnies age for many years in cask

Vinho Verde.agingRules: No ageing mandate; usually drunk young

Alentejo.classification: DOC Alentejo and Vinho Regional Alentejano

Mosel.climate: Cool; steep slate slopes above the river catch the sun
Mosel.agingRules: No ageing mandate; Prädikat levels are set by grape ripeness at harvest

Rheingau.climate: Cool, south-facing slopes along the Rhine

Pfalz.climate: One of Germany's warmest and driest regions

Wachau.classification: DAC, with its own Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd ripeness terms
Wachau.climate: Cool continental along the Danube, with warm days and cold nights

Tokaj.classification: Tokaj protected designation, with Aszú graded by sweetness
Tokaj.climate: Continental; autumn mists encourage noble rot
Tokaj.agingRules: Tokaji Aszú must age at least 3 years, with 18 months in cask

Santorini.climate: Hot, dry and windy island; vines trained low in basket shapes
Santorini.agingRules: No general ageing mandate; Vinsanto is aged for years

Sonoma County.classification: AVAs including Russian River Valley, Alexander Valley and Sonoma Coast
Sonoma County.climate: Varied: fog-cooled near the coast, warm inland

Central Coast.classification: AVAs including Paso Robles, Santa Rita Hills and Santa Lucia Highlands
Central Coast.climate: Cool Pacific influence in the south; warmer inland at Paso Robles

Willamette Valley.classification: AVA, with nested AVAs such as Dundee Hills
Willamette Valley.climate: Cool and wet, with dry summers

Columbia Valley.classification: AVA covering most of Washington State's vineyards
Columbia Valley.climate: Dry, sunny desert with long summer days

Niagara Peninsula.climate: Cool continental, moderated by Lake Ontario; famous for icewine
Niagara Peninsula.agingRules: No general ageing mandate; icewine grapes must freeze naturally on the vine

Okanagan Valley.climate: Dry and sunny in summer, with hot days and cool nights

Maipo Valley.climate: Warm Mediterranean, cooled by air from the Andes

Casablanca Valley.climate: Cool, with morning fog from the Pacific

Mendoza.classification: DOC Luján de Cuyo and other sub-regions
Mendoza.climate: High-altitude desert: sunny, dry, with cold nights

McLaren Vale.climate: Warm Mediterranean, cooled by the sea

Hunter Valley.climate: Hot and humid, with summer rain
Hunter Valley.agingRules: No ageing mandate; Hunter Sémillon is known for ageing for decades

Coonawarra.climate: Cool, with famous red terra rossa soil over limestone

Central Otago.climate: The world's most southerly wine region: continental, dry, with big day-night swings

Hawke's Bay.climate: Warm and sunny for New Zealand

Stellenbosch.climate: Warm Mediterranean, cooled by False Bay

Swartland.climate: Hot and dry, with many old bush vines

Dalmatia.classification: Protected designations such as Dingač and Postup

Franciacorta.climate: Mild, moderated by Lake Iseo and the morainic hills south of it
Franciacorta.agingRules: Non-vintage: min 18 months on lees. Satèn and Rosé: 24. Vintage (Millesimato): 30. Riserva: 60.

England.classification: PDO English Quality Sparkling Wine (traditional method); PGI English for the rest
England.climate: Cool, marginal and maritime, on the same chalk seam as Champagne; the sparkling wines ride on high acidity
England.agingRules: PDO sparkling: min 9 months on lees; most houses give 2 to 5 years

Tasmania.climate: Cool maritime, Australia's coolest wine island; sparkling and Pinot Noir lead
Tasmania.agingRules: No general ageing mandate; traditional-method sparkling commonly sees 2 to 10 years on lees

Tempranillo.profile: Medium-high tannin, red cherry and plum, leather and tobacco with bottle age
Tempranillo.aka: Tinto Fino or Tinta del País in Ribera del Duero, Tinta de Toro in Toro, Tinta Roriz or Aragonez in Portugal
Tempranillo.climate: An early-ripening grape that does best with hot days and cool nights; in cooler spots it keeps fresher acidity and red fruit
Tempranillo.winemaking: Often aged in oak; American oak gives the dill, coconut and vanilla of traditional Rioja, French oak a more polished, spicy style
Tempranillo.food: Roast lamb, chorizo and jamón, grilled meats and hard cheeses such as Manchego
Tempranillo.ageing: Rioja's Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva labels show how long it was aged before release; good examples age into leather, tobacco and dried fruit
Tempranillo.lookalike: Softer and less tannic than Cabernet Sauvignon, with more red fruit and savoury leather notes
Tempranillo.blends: Often blended with Garnacha, Graciano or Mazuelo (Carignan) in Rioja; one of the main grapes in Port

Cabernet Sauvignon.profile: High tannin, high acid, blackcurrant and cedar; thick skin gives deep color and structure
Cabernet Sauvignon.climate: Late-ripening, so it needs a warm site; under-ripe fruit tastes of green pepper, warm climates give riper blackcurrant
Cabernet Sauvignon.winemaking: Its tannin suits ageing in new oak, which adds cedar, vanilla and toast
Cabernet Sauvignon.food: Grilled steak, roast lamb and other fatty red meat, which softens its tannin
Cabernet Sauvignon.ageing: One of the longest-ageing reds; tannins soften over years and fruit turns to cedar, tobacco and graphite
Cabernet Sauvignon.lookalike: Firmer and more tannic than Merlot, with blackcurrant rather than plum
Cabernet Sauvignon.blends: The lead grape of Bordeaux Left Bank blends with Merlot and Cabernet Franc, and of Super Tuscans with Sangiovese
Cabernet Sauvignon.origin: Bordeaux, where it arose as a natural cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc

Pinot Noir.profile: Light body, high acid, low tannin; red cherry and forest floor, thin-skinned and site-transparent
Pinot Noir.aka: Pinot Nero in Italy, Spätburgunder in Germany, Blauburgunder in Austria
Pinot Noir.climate: Needs a cool climate; too much heat makes it jammy and flat, cool sites keep it fragrant
Pinot Noir.winemaking: Thin skins make it hard to grow; winemakers handle it gently and use oak lightly so the fruit shows
Pinot Noir.food: Duck, mushrooms, salmon and roast chicken: a red that can go with fish
Pinot Noir.ageing: The best age into earthy, forest-floor and mushroom notes; simpler ones are best young
Pinot Noir.lookalike: Lighter in colour and tannin than Merlot or Cabernet, with red rather than black fruit
Pinot Noir.blends: A main grape of Champagne and other traditional-method sparkling wine, alongside Chardonnay
Pinot Noir.origin: Burgundy, where it has grown for centuries
wines: Oregon and New Zealand Pinot Noir

Chardonnay.profile: Neutral grape that takes on winemaking choices readily — oak gives vanilla/butter, steel keeps it lean and citrus
Chardonnay.aka: Called by its region in Burgundy: Chablis, Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet and Mâcon are all Chardonnay
Chardonnay.climate: Grows almost anywhere; cool climates give green apple, citrus and high acidity, warm ones peach, pineapple and tropical fruit
Chardonnay.winemaking: Malolactic fermentation turns sharp acid creamy and can add a buttery note; lees ageing adds texture
Chardonnay.food: Oaked styles suit roast chicken, lobster and creamy sauces; unoaked ones suit oysters and white fish
Chardonnay.ageing: Top Burgundy whites age for a decade or more, gaining nutty, toasty notes
Chardonnay.lookalike: Fuller and rounder than Sauvignon Blanc, with less herbaceous aroma
Chardonnay.blends: Blanc de Blancs Champagne is 100% Chardonnay; it's also in most Champagne blends
Chardonnay.origin: Burgundy, a cross of Pinot and Gouais Blanc

notes: Green-gold berries in small, compact bunches

Sauvignon Blanc.profile: High acid, herbaceous, gooseberry and passionfruit; pyrazines drive the grassy, cut-grass note
Sauvignon Blanc.aka: Fumé Blanc on some Californian labels; Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé in the Loire are Sauvignon Blanc
Sauvignon Blanc.climate: Prefers cool climates that keep its acidity and green, grassy aromas; warmer sites push it towards tropical fruit
Sauvignon Blanc.winemaking: Usually fermented cold in steel to keep its aromas; some, like Pouilly-Fumé or Bordeaux whites, see oak
Sauvignon Blanc.food: Goat's cheese, salads, asparagus, green herbs and shellfish
Sauvignon Blanc.ageing: Mostly made to drink young and fresh
Sauvignon Blanc.lookalike: Sharper and greener than Chardonnay; often compared with Verdejo and Grüner Veltliner
Sauvignon Blanc.blends: Blended with Sémillon in white Bordeaux and sweet Sauternes
Sauvignon Blanc.origin: Western France: the Loire and Bordeaux

Nebbiolo.profile: High tannin AND high acid, pale color despite intensity; tar and rose petal aromatics, needs years to soften
Nebbiolo.aka: Spanna in northern Piedmont, Chiavennasca in Valtellina
Nebbiolo.climate: Late-ripening and fussy about site; it does best on the foggy, sunny hillsides of the Langhe in Piedmont
Nebbiolo.winemaking: Traditionally aged in large old casks; Barolo and Barbaresco have legal minimum ageing before release
Nebbiolo.food: Truffles, braised beef, game and rich pasta such as tajarin with ragù
Nebbiolo.ageing: Among the slowest-maturing reds; Barolo often needs ten years or more to soften
Nebbiolo.lookalike: Pale like Pinot Noir but far more tannic; Greece's Xinomavro is often compared with it

notes: Pale skins for such a tannic grape

Grenache.profile: Low tannin, high alcohol, red berry and white pepper; base grape of most dry Provençal rosé
Grenache.aka: Garnacha in Spain, Cannonau in Sardinia
Grenache.climate: Loves heat and drought; it ripens to high sugar, so the wines are often high in alcohol
Grenache.winemaking: Often made without much new oak to keep its red fruit; also widely made into rosé
Grenache.food: Roast meats, barbecue, stews and Mediterranean dishes with herbs
Grenache.ageing: Fruity young wines are for drinking early; old-vine Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Priorat can age well
Grenache.lookalike: Paler and softer than Syrah, with red berry rather than black fruit and pepper
Grenache.blends: The G in GSM blends with Syrah and Mourvèdre; the main grape of Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Provence rosé

notes: Thin skins, so a paler wine

Syrah.profile: Deep color, medium-high tannin, black pepper and blackberry, smoky at altitude
Syrah.aka: Shiraz in Australia and South Africa
Syrah.climate: Cool sites like the Northern Rhône give black pepper and olive; hot ones like the Barossa give ripe, jammy blackberry
Syrah.winemaking: Sometimes co-fermented with a little Viognier for perfume, as in Côte-Rôtie
Syrah.food: Grilled and barbecued meat, lamb, game and peppery dishes
Syrah.ageing: Hermitage and the best Shiraz age for many years into smoky, meaty notes
Syrah.lookalike: Darker and spicier than Grenache; Petite Sirah is a different grape, a cross of Syrah and Peloursin
Syrah.blends: The S in GSM; blended with Cabernet Sauvignon in Australia

Riesling.profile: High acid, aromatic, can be bone-dry to very sweet; ages into petrol/TDN character that's a feature, not a fault
Riesling.aka: Sometimes labelled Rhine Riesling or Johannisberg Riesling
Riesling.climate: Thrives in cool climates such as the Mosel, keeping high acidity even when very ripe
Riesling.winemaking: Almost never oaked; German labels such as Kabinett and Spätlese describe ripeness at harvest, and 'trocken' means dry
Riesling.food: Spicy Asian food, pork, and off-dry styles with sweet-and-sour dishes
Riesling.ageing: Its acidity lets it age for decades, developing honey and the petrol (TDN) note
Riesling.lookalike: More aromatic and acidic than Chardonnay; drier and sharper than Gewürztraminer
Riesling.blends: Almost always bottled on its own

notes: Small green berries in compact bunches

Merlot.profile: Softer tannin than Cabernet, plum and cocoa, ripens earlier; the backbone of Right Bank Bordeaux
Merlot.climate: Ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon, so it suits cooler clay soils like Bordeaux's Right Bank; too hot and it turns jammy
Merlot.winemaking: Often aged in oak, which adds chocolate and vanilla to its plum fruit
Merlot.food: Roast pork, duck, mushroom dishes and pasta with meat sauce
Merlot.ageing: The best Pomerol and Saint-Émilion age well; everyday Merlot is for drinking within a few years
Merlot.lookalike: Softer and rounder than Cabernet Sauvignon, with plum rather than blackcurrant
Merlot.blends: The main grape of Bordeaux Right Bank blends, with Cabernet Franc

Malbec.profile: Deep color, medium-high tannin, black plum and blackberry with a violet edge; softer and riper in Argentina's high-altitude sun than in its native Cahors
Malbec.climate: High-altitude vineyards in Mendoza give intense sun with cool nights, so it ripens fully while keeping freshness
Malbec.winemaking: Often aged in oak, adding vanilla and chocolate
Malbec.food: Grilled beef, the classic Argentine asado, and spicy sausage
Malbec.ageing: Most is made to drink young; top Cahors and Mendoza examples age well
Malbec.lookalike: Juicier and softer than Cabernet Sauvignon, with a violet perfume
Malbec.blends: A minor grape in Bordeaux blends; usually on its own in Argentina

Zinfandel.profile: High alcohol, jammy black and red fruit, peppery spice; sensitive to uneven ripening within a single cluster
Zinfandel.aka: Primitivo in southern Italy; also Crljenak Kaštelanski in Croatia, where it came from
Zinfandel.climate: Thrives in warm California; its bunches ripen unevenly, so some berries raisin before others are ripe
Zinfandel.winemaking: Also made into pale, sweetish 'White Zinfandel' rosé
Zinfandel.food: Barbecue, burgers, pizza and spicy sausage
Zinfandel.ageing: Mostly for drinking young; old-vine examples can age a few years
Zinfandel.lookalike: Jammier and higher in alcohol than Merlot; Petite Sirah is often blended in for colour and tannin
Zinfandel.blends: Old California 'field blends' mix it with Petite Sirah and Carignan
Zinfandel.origin: Croatia, where it's called Crljenak Kaštelanski

notes: Berries in one bunch ripen unevenly

Sangiovese.profile: High acid, medium tannin, sour cherry and dried herb with a savory, earthy edge; the backbone of most Tuscan reds
Sangiovese.aka: Brunello in Montalcino, Prugnolo Gentile in Montepulciano, Morellino in Maremma
Sangiovese.climate: Needs warmth to ripen but keeps high acidity; Tuscany's hillsides suit it
Sangiovese.winemaking: Traditionally aged in large casks; Brunello di Montalcino has a long minimum ageing before release
Sangiovese.food: Tomato-based dishes, pizza, pasta and grilled steak (bistecca alla fiorentina)
Sangiovese.ageing: Chianti Classico Riserva and Brunello age well into dried cherry, leather and earth
Sangiovese.lookalike: Higher in acid and more savoury than Merlot; lighter than Cabernet Sauvignon
Sangiovese.blends: The main grape of Chianti; blended with Cabernet and Merlot in Super Tuscans

Cabernet Franc.profile: Lighter and more aromatic than Cabernet Sauvignon, with red fruit, violet, and a distinct green-pepper (pyrazine) note
Cabernet Franc.aka: Breton in the Loire; Chinon and Bourgueil are Cabernet Franc
Cabernet Franc.climate: Ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon, so it does well in cooler places like the Loire
Cabernet Franc.winemaking: In the Loire it's often made with little new oak to keep its fresh, leafy character
Cabernet Franc.food: Roast pork, charcuterie, goat's cheese and dishes with herbs
Cabernet Franc.ageing: Light Loire styles are for drinking young; Saint-Émilion's best blends age for years
Cabernet Franc.lookalike: Lighter, more fragrant and leafier than Cabernet Sauvignon, one of its parents
Cabernet Franc.blends: A key partner of Merlot on Bordeaux's Right Bank, as in Saint-Émilion
Cabernet Franc.origin: South-west France and the Basque Country

Petit Verdot.profile: Deep color, high tannin, dense dark fruit and floral violet notes; used mostly as a small blending component for structure
Petit Verdot.climate: Ripens very late, so in Bordeaux it often struggles; warmer places like Australia and Spain ripen it fully
Petit Verdot.winemaking: Used in small amounts for colour, tannin and violet perfume
Petit Verdot.food: Rich grilled and roast red meats
Petit Verdot.ageing: Adds structure that helps Bordeaux blends age
Petit Verdot.lookalike: Darker and more tannic than Cabernet Sauvignon
Petit Verdot.blends: A small part of many Bordeaux blends; occasionally bottled alone in warm regions

Carignan.profile: High acid and tannin when young, red fruit and earthy rusticity; old vines soften into more concentrated, balanced wines
Carignan.aka: Cariñena or Mazuelo in Spain, Carignano in Sardinia
Carignan.climate: Needs heat and a long season; very productive unless yields are kept low
Carignan.winemaking: Sometimes made by carbonic maceration to soften its tannin
Carignan.food: Hearty stews, cassoulet and grilled meats
Carignan.ageing: Old-vine examples from Priorat and the Languedoc can age well
Carignan.lookalike: More rustic and acidic than Grenache, which it's often blended with
Carignan.blends: Blended with Grenache and Syrah in the Languedoc and Priorat; Mazuelo plays a small part in Rioja
Carignan.origin: Aragón, Spain, around the town of Cariñena

Mourvèdre.profile: Deep color, high tannin, dark fruit with gamey, earthy, and leather notes; needs warmth to ripen fully
Mourvèdre.aka: Monastrell in Spain, Mataro in Australia
Mourvèdre.climate: Needs a hot site to ripen; Bandol by the sea in Provence is its classic home
Mourvèdre.winemaking: Bandol reds must be mostly Mourvèdre and spend time in oak
Mourvèdre.food: Game, lamb with herbs, beef stew and grilled sausages
Mourvèdre.ageing: Bandol reds need years to soften and age into savoury, gamey notes
Mourvèdre.lookalike: Meatier and more tannic than Grenache
Mourvèdre.blends: The M in GSM; also part of Bandol rosé

notes: Small, thick-skinned berries in tight bunches

Barbera.profile: Very high acid, low tannin, bright red cherry and plum; food-friendly and rarely needs long aging
Barbera.aka: Barbera d'Asti and Barbera d'Alba name it by town
Barbera.climate: Ripens earlier than Nebbiolo, so Piedmont growers give it the less prized sites
Barbera.winemaking: Its low tannin means it's often aged in small oak barrels, which add a little structure
Barbera.food: Tomato sauces, pizza, salami and fatty dishes its acidity cuts through
Barbera.ageing: Best young to medium-aged, for its fruit
Barbera.lookalike: Much softer in tannin than Nebbiolo from the same hills, with more acidity than Merlot

Gamay.profile: Light body, low tannin, bright red fruit (strawberry, cherry) often with a light carbonic, banana-like note from carbonic maceration
Gamay.aka: Gamay Noir; Beaujolais and the Beaujolais crus such as Morgon and Fleurie are Gamay
Gamay.climate: Suits the granite hills of Beaujolais; ripens early
Gamay.winemaking: Whole bunches are often fermented by carbonic maceration, giving soft, fruity wine
Gamay.food: Charcuterie, roast chicken, salads; good lightly chilled
Gamay.ageing: Beaujolais Nouveau is meant to be drunk within months; the crus can age several years
Gamay.lookalike: Fruitier and simpler than Pinot Noir, its Burgundy neighbour
Gamay.origin: Burgundy, a cross of Pinot and Gouais Blanc

Montepulciano.profile: Medium-high tannin and acid, dark plum and black cherry with a rustic, earthy edge; not related to the Tuscan town of the same name
Montepulciano.aka: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is the grape; Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese, named after the town
Montepulciano.climate: A warm-climate grape of central and southern Italy
Montepulciano.winemaking: Also made into a deep pink rosé called Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo
Montepulciano.food: Pizza, pasta with meat sauce and grilled lamb
Montepulciano.ageing: Most is for drinking young; the best can age
Montepulciano.lookalike: Softer in acid than Sangiovese, with darker fruit
Montepulciano.blends: Blended with Sangiovese in Rosso Conero and Rosso Piceno

Primitivo.profile: Genetically identical to Zinfandel; high alcohol, jammy dark fruit, dried fig and spice in its southern Italian home
Primitivo.aka: The same grape as Zinfandel in California
Primitivo.climate: Ripens early in hot Puglia, which is where its name comes from (primo, first)
Primitivo.winemaking: Often made rich and ripe, sometimes with a little residual sweetness
Primitivo.food: Barbecue, rich pasta and hard cheeses
Primitivo.lookalike: The same grape as Zinfandel; riper and jammier than Negroamaro, its neighbour in Puglia
Primitivo.blends: Sometimes blended with Negroamaro in Puglia
Primitivo.origin: Croatia; it reached Puglia in the 1700s

notes: Ripens early, and unevenly within a bunch

Touriga Nacional.profile: Deep color, high tannin, concentrated black fruit and violet aromatics; the top grape in Port and increasingly fine dry Douro reds
Touriga Nacional.aka: Tinta Nacional in some parts of Portugal
Touriga Nacional.climate: Thrives in the hot, steep, schist-soil Douro valley
Touriga Nacional.winemaking: For Port, fermentation is stopped with grape spirit, keeping sweetness
Touriga Nacional.food: Dry reds with roast meats and stews; Port with blue cheese and chocolate
Touriga Nacional.ageing: Vintage Port and the best dry reds age for decades
Touriga Nacional.lookalike: More floral and concentrated than Tempranillo (Tinta Roriz), its Douro blending partner
Touriga Nacional.blends: Blended with Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz in Port and Douro reds

Carmenère.profile: Medium tannin, dark fruit with a distinctive green-pepper and herbal note; once confused with Merlot in Chilean vineyards
Carmenère.aka: Once thought to be Merlot in Chile's vineyards
Carmenère.climate: Ripens late and needs a long, warm season; Chile's Central Valley suits it
Carmenère.winemaking: Picked late to soften its green-pepper note
Carmenère.food: Grilled meats, spiced dishes and roasted peppers
Carmenère.ageing: Mostly for drinking within a few years
Carmenère.lookalike: Darker and greener than Merlot, with a herbal, peppery edge
Carmenère.blends: An old Bordeaux grape, now rare there; Chile's signature red

notes: Its leaves turn crimson in autumn

Pinotage.profile: A Pinot Noir x Cinsault cross unique to South Africa; medium tannin, dark berry fruit with a smoky, rubbery note some find polarizing
Pinotage.aka: Only South Africa grows it widely
Pinotage.climate: Ripens early and suits South Africa's warm Western Cape
Pinotage.winemaking: Some producers make a 'coffee' style with heavily toasted oak
Pinotage.ageing: Most is for drinking young; the best can age a decade
Pinotage.lookalike: Darker and more robust than Pinot Noir, one of its parents
Pinotage.blends: Blended with Cabernet and Merlot in 'Cape blends'
Pinotage.origin: South Africa, bred in 1925 from Pinot Noir and Cinsault

Petite Sirah.profile: Deep, almost opaque color, very high tannin, dense black fruit and pepper; often blended with Zinfandel for structure
Petite Sirah.climate: A warm-climate grape, mostly grown in California
Petite Sirah.winemaking: Its dark skins give inky colour and lots of tannin
Petite Sirah.food: Barbecue, braised short ribs and hearty stews
Petite Sirah.ageing: Its tannin lets it age for many years
Petite Sirah.lookalike: Not the same grape as Syrah, but a cross of Syrah and Peloursin; even darker and more tannic
Petite Sirah.blends: Blended with Zinfandel for colour and structure
Petite Sirah.origin: France, bred by Dr Durif in the 1880s

notes: Small berries with very dark skins

Aglianico.profile: High tannin and acid, dark fruit with smoky, tarry, mineral notes; ages slowly and rewards patience
Aglianico.aka: Taurasi and Aglianico del Vulture are named after places
Aglianico.climate: Ripens very late, often on volcanic soils in southern Italy's hills
Aglianico.winemaking: Taurasi has a long minimum ageing before release
Aglianico.food: Braised meats, game and rich ragù
Aglianico.ageing: Slow to mature; the best need years to soften
Aglianico.lookalike: Often compared to Nebbiolo for its high tannin and acid

Corvina.profile: Light-to-medium tannin, tart cherry fruit; the main grape of Valpolicella, transformed into rich, raisined character when dried for Amarone
Corvina.aka: Corvina Veronese; the main grape of Valpolicella, Amarone and Bardolino
Corvina.climate: Grows in the hills north of Verona near Lake Garda
Corvina.winemaking: For Amarone, the grapes are dried for months (appassimento) before fermenting, concentrating sugar and flavour
Corvina.food: Light Valpolicella with pasta and salumi; Amarone with braised beef and aged cheese
Corvina.ageing: Light Valpolicella is for drinking young; Amarone ages for many years
Corvina.lookalike: Lighter than most reds when fresh, like a tart-cherry Pinot Noir
Corvina.blends: Blended with Corvinone and Rondinella in Valpolicella and Amarone

Cinsault.profile: Low tannin, pale color, soft red berry fruit; used mostly for easy-drinking reds and as a rosé base blended with Grenache
Cinsault.climate: Copes well with heat and drought in southern France and South Africa
Cinsault.winemaking: Often made into rosé or light reds
Cinsault.food: Rosé with salads and seafood; light reds with charcuterie
Cinsault.lookalike: Paler and softer than Grenache, its common blending partner
Cinsault.blends: With Grenache in Provence rosé; one of the parents of Pinotage

Pinot Grigio.profile: Neutral to lightly aromatic, high acid, pear and citrus; usually made lean and crisp in Italy, richer and more textured as Pinot Gris in Alsace
Pinot Grigio.aka: Pinot Gris in France, Grauburgunder in Germany
Pinot Grigio.climate: Grows widely; cool northern Italy gives crisp wines, warmer Alsace richer, spicier ones
Pinot Grigio.winemaking: Italian Pinot Grigio is picked early and made crisp in steel; Alsace Pinot Gris is riper and fuller
Pinot Grigio.food: Light seafood, salads and antipasti; Alsace Pinot Gris with richer dishes
Pinot Grigio.ageing: Mostly for drinking young; Alsace versions can age
Pinot Grigio.lookalike: Its skin is greyish pink; a colour mutation of Pinot Noir, like Pinot Blanc
Pinot Grigio.blends: Usually bottled on its own; skin contact can make it copper-coloured 'ramato'
Pinot Grigio.origin: Burgundy, a colour mutation of Pinot Noir

Viognier.profile: Low acid, full body, heavily perfumed with apricot, honeysuckle, and stone fruit
Viognier.aka: Condrieu in the Northern Rhône is Viognier
Viognier.climate: Needs warmth to ripen and develop its perfume, but too much heat makes it flabby
Viognier.winemaking: Often given some oak or lees ageing for texture
Viognier.food: Mildly spiced dishes, apricot-glazed chicken and creamy curries
Viognier.ageing: Best young, while its perfume is fresh
Viognier.lookalike: More perfumed and lower in acid than Chardonnay
Viognier.blends: A little is co-fermented with Syrah in Côte-Rôtie for aroma

Gewürztraminer.profile: Very aromatic, low acid, lychee and rose petal with a hint of spice; often has noticeable residual sugar
Gewürztraminer.aka: An aromatic form of the old Traminer grape; 'Gewürz' means spice in German
Gewürztraminer.climate: Prefers cool regions like Alsace; its pink skin ripens early
Gewürztraminer.winemaking: Often left off-dry; late-harvest versions are sweet
Gewürztraminer.food: Spicy Asian food, Munster cheese and foie gras
Gewürztraminer.lookalike: More perfumed and lower in acid than Riesling
Gewürztraminer.origin: The Traminer family, named after Tramin in northern Italy

Chenin Blanc.profile: High acid, versatile across dry, off-dry, sweet, and sparkling styles; honey and quince notes intensify with botrytis or age
Chenin Blanc.aka: Steen in South Africa; Vouvray and Savennières are Chenin Blanc
Chenin Blanc.climate: Grows from the cool Loire to warm South Africa, keeping high acidity
Chenin Blanc.winemaking: Made dry (sec), off-dry (demi-sec), sweet (moelleux) and sparkling (Crémant de Loire)
Chenin Blanc.food: Pork, chicken, Thai dishes and fruit tarts with sweet styles
Chenin Blanc.ageing: Its acidity lets the best age for decades
Chenin Blanc.lookalike: Higher in acid than Chardonnay, with apple, quince and honey

notes: Thin skins, prone to noble rot

Albariño.profile: High acid, medium body, stone fruit and citrus with a distinct saline, coastal minerality
Albariño.climate: Grows in rainy, cool Galicia on the Atlantic coast
Albariño.winemaking: Usually fermented in steel to keep it fresh; some see lees ageing
Albariño.lookalike: Fuller and more peachy than Vinho Verde blends; saltier than Sauvignon Blanc
Albariño.blends: Bottled alone in Rías Baixas; blended in Vinho Verde
Albariño.origin: Galicia in north-west Spain, or just over the border in Portugal

Grüner Veltliner.profile: High acid, white pepper and citrus with a lentil-like savory note; ranges from light quaffable to age-worthy Smaragd bottlings
Grüner Veltliner.climate: Austria's cool Danube valley suits it
Grüner Veltliner.winemaking: Wachau labels its levels by ripeness: Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd, the richest
Grüner Veltliner.food: Schnitzel, asparagus, salads and Asian dishes
Grüner Veltliner.ageing: Light ones are for drinking young; Smaragd can age a decade
Grüner Veltliner.lookalike: Peppery and more savoury than Sauvignon Blanc

Muscat.profile: Intensely floral and grapey — the only grape family that actually tastes like fresh grapes; ranges from light and fizzy to sweet fortified styles
Muscat.aka: Moscato in Italy, Moscatel in Spain and Portugal; a family of related grapes
Muscat.climate: Grows in warm and cool places; different members suit different climates
Muscat.winemaking: Made dry in Alsace, lightly sparkling in Moscato d'Asti and fortified in Rutherglen and Beaumes-de-Venise
Muscat.food: Fruit desserts; dry Alsace Muscat with asparagus
Muscat.ageing: Fresh styles are for drinking young; fortified ones age for years
Muscat.lookalike: Tastes of fresh grapes, unlike almost any other wine; Torrontés is similarly floral
Muscat.origin: One of the oldest grape families, from the eastern Mediterranean

Sémillon.profile: Low acid on its own, waxy texture, honeyed and lanolin notes; prone to botrytis, which makes it central to Sauternes' sweet wines
Sémillon.aka: Semillon without the accent in Australia
Sémillon.climate: Prone to noble rot (botrytis) in misty Sauternes autumns
Sémillon.winemaking: Hunter Valley Semillon is picked early, low in alcohol and unoaked
Sémillon.food: Seafood with dry styles; blue cheese and desserts with Sauternes
Sémillon.ageing: Hunter Valley Semillon ages into toast and honey; Sauternes ages for decades
Sémillon.lookalike: Waxier and softer than Sauvignon Blanc, its usual partner
Sémillon.blends: Blended with Sauvignon Blanc in white Bordeaux and Sauternes

notes: Golden, thin skins, prone to noble rot

Vermentino.profile: High acid, light body, citrus and herbal notes with a faint bitter almond finish; a classic Mediterranean seafood white
Vermentino.aka: Rolle in Provence, Pigato in Liguria
Vermentino.climate: A Mediterranean grape that likes sun and sea air
Vermentino.winemaking: Usually fermented in steel and made fresh
Vermentino.lookalike: Lighter and more herbal than Viognier
Vermentino.blends: Part of many Provence rosés and whites

Verdejo.profile: High acid, herbal and fennel notes with a slightly bitter almond finish; often compared to Sauvignon Blanc but softer
Verdejo.climate: Grows on Spain's high, sunny plateau, where cool nights keep it fresh
Verdejo.winemaking: Usually picked at night and kept cool to protect its aromas
Verdejo.lookalike: Often compared with Sauvignon Blanc, but softer with a bitter almond finish
Verdejo.blends: Sometimes blended with Sauvignon Blanc in Rueda

Torrontés.profile: Highly aromatic, floral and citrus notes similar to Muscat, but with more body and a drier finish
Torrontés.climate: Grows in Salta's very high vineyards, where cool nights keep it fresh
Torrontés.food: Spicy food, empanadas and Asian dishes
Torrontés.lookalike: Smells like Muscat, one of its parents, but tastes drier
Torrontés.origin: Argentina, a cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica

Marsanne.profile: Full body, low acid, nutty and honeysuckle notes; typically blended with Roussanne for texture and lift
Marsanne.aka: Part of white Hermitage, Saint-Joseph and Crozes-Hermitage
Marsanne.winemaking: Sometimes oaked; gains weight with lees ageing
Marsanne.food: Roast chicken, creamy dishes and richer fish
Marsanne.ageing: Can age well, gaining nutty, honeyed notes
Marsanne.lookalike: Fuller and lower in acid than Roussanne
Marsanne.blends: Blended with Roussanne in the Rhône

Roussanne.profile: Aromatic, higher acid than Marsanne, with pear, herbal tea, and honey notes; adds finesse when blended
Roussanne.aka: Part of white Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Hermitage
Roussanne.climate: Ripens late and is prone to disease, so it's harder to grow than Marsanne
Roussanne.winemaking: Often fermented in oak for texture
Roussanne.food: Poultry, pork and rich fish dishes
Roussanne.lookalike: More aromatic and acidic than Marsanne
Roussanne.blends: With Marsanne in the Rhône and in white Châteauneuf-du-Pape

notes: Russet skins when ripe: 'roux' means red-brown

Assyrtiko.profile: Very high acid, citrus and mineral with a distinct smoky, flinty edge from volcanic soils
Assyrtiko.climate: Grows in Santorini's volcanic soil, with vines trained into low baskets (kouloura) against the wind
Assyrtiko.winemaking: Usually unoaked; Nykteri is a richer, often oaked style; Vinsanto is sweet, from sun-dried grapes
Assyrtiko.food: Grilled fish, shellfish and Greek salads
Assyrtiko.ageing: Keeps its acidity and can age well
Assyrtiko.lookalike: Sharper and saltier than most Mediterranean whites

notes: Vines trained into low baskets against the wind

Furmint.profile: High acid, orchard fruit and honey notes; the backbone grape of both dry Hungarian whites and sweet botrytized Tokaji
Furmint.climate: Prone to noble rot in Tokaj's misty autumns
Furmint.winemaking: Botrytised berries (aszú) are added to wine to make sweet Tokaji Aszú
Furmint.food: Dry styles with pork and paprika dishes; sweet Tokaji with foie gras and desserts
Furmint.ageing: Tokaji Aszú can age for decades
Furmint.lookalike: Fuller and smokier than Riesling, with similar high acidity

notes: Thin skins, prone to noble rot

Garganega.profile: Medium acid, almond and citrus blossom notes; the main grape behind Soave
Garganega.climate: Grows in volcanic hills east of Verona
Garganega.winemaking: Also dried to make sweet Recioto di Soave
Garganega.food: Seafood risotto, light pasta and antipasti
Garganega.ageing: Mostly young; Soave Classico can age a few years
Garganega.lookalike: Softer than Pinot Grigio, with almond and citrus
Garganega.blends: Sometimes blended with Trebbiano di Soave

Fiano.profile: Medium-high acid, honeyed and nutty notes with a floral lift; one of southern Italy's more textured whites
Fiano.aka: Fiano di Avellino names it by town
Fiano.climate: Grows in the hills of Campania
Fiano.winemaking: Usually unoaked; gains texture with lees ageing
Fiano.food: Seafood pasta, grilled fish and mozzarella
Fiano.ageing: Can age several years into honeyed notes

Pinot Blanc.profile: A lighter, less aromatic mutation of Pinot Gris; crisp apple and citrus with a neutral, food-friendly profile
Pinot Blanc.aka: Pinot Bianco in Italy, Weissburgunder in Germany and Austria
Pinot Blanc.winemaking: Usually unoaked; also used for Crémant d'Alsace sparkling wine
Pinot Blanc.food: Light dishes, quiche and white fish
Pinot Blanc.lookalike: Softer and less aromatic than Pinot Gris
Pinot Blanc.origin: Burgundy, a colour mutation of Pinot Noir

Melon de Bourgogne.profile: Neutral and high acid on its own; the grape behind Muscadet, often given texture through extended lees aging (sur lie)
Melon de Bourgogne.climate: Grows near the Atlantic at the mouth of the Loire
Melon de Bourgogne.winemaking: Aged on its lees (sur lie) to gain texture and a slight spritz
Melon de Bourgogne.ageing: For drinking young; the best can age
Melon de Bourgogne.lookalike: Even more neutral than Pinot Blanc
Melon de Bourgogne.blends: Bottled on its own as Muscadet
Melon de Bourgogne.origin: Burgundy; it moved to the Loire after the great frost of 1709

Trebbiano.profile: High-yielding, neutral and high-acid; Italy's most-planted white, usually made into simple, crisp everyday wine
Trebbiano.aka: Ugni Blanc in France, where it's distilled into Cognac and Armagnac
Trebbiano.climate: Grows almost anywhere and yields heavily
Trebbiano.winemaking: Mostly made into simple, crisp wine; also distilled into brandy
Trebbiano.lookalike: Even more neutral than Pinot Grigio
Trebbiano.blends: Part of Orvieto and many everyday central Italian whites

Xinomavro.profile: High acid and tannin, red fruit with tomato-leaf and olive notes; often compared to Nebbiolo for its structure and aging potential
Xinomavro.climate: Grows in cool northern Greece, around Naoussa
Xinomavro.food: Lamb, tomato-based dishes and hard cheeses
Xinomavro.ageing: Ages for many years, like Nebbiolo
Xinomavro.lookalike: Often compared with Nebbiolo for its pale colour, high acid and tannin

Zweigelt.profile: A Blaufränkisch x St. Laurent cross unique to Austria; light-to-medium tannin, cherry and pepper notes
Zweigelt.climate: Ripens early in Austria's cool climate
Zweigelt.winemaking: Made light and fruity, or richer with oak
Zweigelt.lookalike: Juicier and softer than Blaufränkisch, one of its parents
Zweigelt.origin: Austria, bred in 1922 by Fritz Zweigelt

vanilla.cause: Lactones from oak barrel aging, concentrated in American oak

coconut.cause: Same oak-lactone family as vanilla — a signature of American oak specifically

butter.cause: Diacetyl, a byproduct of malolactic fermentation converting malic acid to lactic acid

petrol.cause: TDN (a naphthalene compound) forming as Riesling ages — a hallmark of mature examples, not a flaw

smoke.cause: Guaiacol and related phenols from toasted oak, or naturally in grapes grown in volcanic/mineral soils

leather.cause: Tertiary aromas from prolonged bottle age and slow oxidation, common in aged Tempranillo and Nebbiolo

green pepper.cause: Pyrazines, most concentrated in Cabernet Franc, Sauvignon Blanc, and under-ripe Cabernet Sauvignon

tropical fruit.cause: Thiols released during fermentation, especially pronounced in warm-climate Sauvignon Blanc and Chenin Blanc

honey.cause: Botrytis (noble rot) concentrating sugars, or simple bottle-age oxidation in aromatic whites

brioche.cause: Autolysis — dead yeast cells breaking down during extended lees aging, classic in traditional-method sparkling
